extracted.subtask_short: Checking whether claimant-supplied evidence supports a political claim
extracted.subtask_description: Determining whether the evidence a claimant supplies actually supports the specific factual claim they made, and if not, resolving the claim against a domain-appropriate primary source of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger is a factual assertion, not opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff systematically review transcripts and video of political speech (Sunday shows, C-SPAN, campaign ads, presidential remarks, congressional statements) looking for statements presented as fact — the trigger for further work is a factual assertion, not an opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage claimant directly for response or supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a statement is flagged as possibly inaccurate or misleading, the outlet attempts to engage directly with the person or organization who made the claim, giving them the opportunity to respond or provide support before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof is on the claimant
rubrics_metrics.description: "The burden is on the person or organization making the claim to provide the evidence to support it." FactCheck.org first asks the claimant (or their staff/office) for their sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage claim-verification algorithm: relevance check then independent research
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage A: if the claimant provides supporting material, FactCheck.org checks whether that material actually supports the claim as stated (rather than merely being related to the topic) — a claim is judged adequately supported when the evidence the claimant provides holds up, and no further independent research is conducted in that case. Stage B: if the supporting material does not actually support the claim, or if no evidence is provided at all, FactCheck.org conducts its own independent research, relying on primary sources first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-indexed primary source hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: FactCheck.org explicitly lists the categories of primary source it relies on, in preference to secondary reporting or press releases: the Library of Congress, for congressional testimony records; the House Clerk and Senate Secretary's offices, for official roll-call vote records; the Bureau of Labor Statistics, for employment and price data; the SEC, IRS, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and Energy Information Administration, for financial and economic data specific to their domains; nonpartisan government analytic bodies — the CBO, GAO, and CRS — treated as authoritative, nonpartisan intermediaries between raw data and a checkable conclusion; "respected and trustworthy outside experts" (the Kaiser Family Foundation is cited as an example in the health-policy domain) when the topic requires subject-matter expertise the staff does not have in-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screen for statements based on facts vs. non-checkable statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The methodology reiterates that the target is statements "based on facts" — the outlet's stated purpose is to "focus on claims that are false or misleading," implying an initial screen that filters out claims for which the claimant's own supplied evidence turns out to be adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent fact-checking layer separate from the original reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: Every published item goes through four sequential review layers before publication: line editing; copy editing; fact-checking (an independent check of the piece's own claims and citations, separate from the original researching reporter); director-level review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlink all sources for reader replicability
rubrics_metrics.description: All sources used are hyperlinked directly in the published piece, so that a reader can independently follow the same evidentiary chain the reporter did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct when new information materially changes the story
rubrics_metrics.description: "If any new information comes to light after we publish a story that materially changes that story," FactCheck.org will clarify, correct, or update it, accompanied by an explanatory note stating why the change was made and the date it occurred — corrections are appended and dated rather than silently edited in place.
